FLASHCARD SET · AGES 6–12 WEEKS

Faces & Visual Tracking Flashcards

Twelve cards for the second newborn stage: friendly faces, bold patterns and the very first hints of red, made for slow, close, parent-led looking.

These cards belong to Newborn 2 on the Kiddo School learning path.

THE CARDS

Every card in the set.

Each card has its own page: the picture and short, practical notes for grown-ups — what it is for, how to use it, how to print it. Tap any card to open it.

HOW TO USE THESE CARDS

Four ways that work.

You do not need a plan or a printer schedule. Pick one idea, try it for two minutes and see what happens.

  1. 01

    Slow is the whole trick

    Move a card a few centimetres side to side and let your baby’s eyes follow. At this age slow movement is fascinating — quick movement is invisible.

  2. 02

    Faces first

    Babies love faces more than anything. Start with the face cards and let your baby study them before trying the patterns.

  3. 03

    Name what they see

    Say the word softly as your baby looks — eyes, stripes, wavy. The words matter less than your voice staying warm and close.

  4. 04

    Stop while it is fun

    Two or three cards is a full session at this age. Ending while your baby is still interested makes tomorrow’s session easy.

      Eyes Flashcard for Babies

      Two big friendly eyes, drawn in bold black and white. Faces are the first thing babies love to look at, and eyes are the part they study longest — this card gives your baby exactly that, up close.

      Why black and white works

      Gives brand-new eyes one bold, easy target to lock onto in the first blurry weeks.

      Show it slowly

      Hold it a hand's width from your baby, drift one slow inch, then rest.

      What it builds

      Steady staring builds the eye muscles that focusing and later tracking depend on.

      Print it like this

      Print on bright white cardstock so the black edges stay crisp.

      Baby tip

      Two calm minutes are plenty; stop while the gaze is still fresh.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Eyes lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks class on the Learning Path.

      Happy face Flashcard for Babies

      A big bold smiley face in high contrast. At 6–12 weeks many babies give their first real social smiles, and a clear happy face like this one often brings one out.

      Why black and white works

      Offers a smile your baby can meet, since faces pull newborn attention more than anything else.

      Show it slowly

      Show it slowly, one long pause between card and your own smiling face.

      What it builds

      Watching expressions seeds early social attention and the first back-and-forth smiles.

      Print it like this

      Cardstock, sharp corners trimmed, sized to hold comfortably in one hand.

      Baby tip

      Smile at your baby too — your face is the second picture.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Happy face lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks class on the Learning Path.

      Different face Flashcard for Babies

      A second face with a different expression, so your baby can compare two faces side by side over the week. Noticing “same” and “different” is very early thinking, built one card at a time.

      Why black and white works

      Shows a second expression so comparing one face with another becomes a tiny workout.

      Show it slowly

      Swap the two faces across a week, placing each calmly in the same spot.

      What it builds

      Noticing differences trains visual discrimination, the skill sorting and matching grow from.

      Print it like this

      Print both faces on matching cardstock so only the expression really differs.

      Baby tip

      No commentary needed; quiet looking does the work at this age.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Different face lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks class on the Learning Path.

      Download card ↓

      Face pattern Flashcard for Babies

      A patterned face where the features are made of bold shapes. It is half face, half pattern — exactly the kind of image that keeps a 6–12-week baby fascinated.

      Why black and white works

      Invites a longer look, because a face made of shapes is doubly interesting to fresh eyes.

      Show it slowly

      Rest it against the changing mat during nappy time and let staring happen.

      What it builds

      Pattern-and-face watching stretches attention span and sharpens edge detection.

      Print it like this

      Use matte cardstock; glossy surfaces catch light and distract young eyes.

      Baby tip

      Nappy-change pauses are a natural slot — short, close and calm.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Face pattern lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks class on the Learning Path.

      Download card ↓

      Concentric circles Flashcard for Babies

      Circles inside circles inside circles, in bold black and white. The gentle rings pull your baby’s eyes inward — lovely, calm tracking practice.

      Why black and white works

      Pulls wandering eyes inward, ring by ring, toward one calm centre.

      Show it slowly

      Lay it down at tummy time and trace one ring slowly with a finger.

      What it builds

      Following rings inward practices smooth eye control and gentle focusing in and out.

      Print it like this

      Trim it edge to edge so the outermost ring touches the border.

      Baby tip

      Trace slower than seems necessary; baby eyes need extra travel time.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Concentric circles lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks class on the Learning Path.

      Wavy lines Flashcard for Babies

      Bold wavy lines rolling across the card. Waves are one of the easiest patterns for young eyes to follow, and they whisper an early idea: things can move smoothly, up and down.

      Why black and white works

      Lets your baby's eyes ride a smooth line, the gentlest possible tracking exercise.

      Show it slowly

      Drift the card in a slow wave across their view, then hold it still.

      What it builds

      Side-to-side following builds the eye teamwork later tracking needs.

      Print it like this

      A4 or A5 cardstock both work; keep the lines bold and unbroken.

      Baby tip

      Two or three waves are enough, then pause for a still stare.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Wavy lines lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks class on the Learning Path.

      Download card ↓

      Zigzag Flashcard for Babies

      A bold zigzag with sharp corners and clear direction changes. After smooth waves, corners are new: your baby’s eyes get a tiny surprise at every turn.

      Why black and white works

      Gives young eyes their first corners, a small step up from smooth waves.

      Show it slowly

      Tap each corner softly with your fingertip, pausing so the gaze can catch up.

      What it builds

      Jumping between corners stretches quick eye movements, an early reading-building skill.

      Print it like this

      Keep cardstock white and uncreased; a bent corner blurs the sharp angles.

      Baby tip

      If staring stops, tip the card slightly and try one fresh corner.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Zigzag lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks class on the Learning Path.

      Large dots Flashcard for Babies

      Big bold dots in a simple arrangement. Dots are friendly: no corners, no direction, just clear round shapes a young baby can rest their eyes on.

      Why black and white works

      Turns simple round dots into a friendly game of looking from one to the next.

      Show it slowly

      Point to each dot in turn during a calm feed, moving your finger gently.

      What it builds

      Hopping glances between dots grow scanning skill and early number sense.

      Print it like this

      Choose thick cardstock so the card survives being gripped or gummed.

      Baby tip

      Let a grabbed card be a win; holding is its own skill.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Large dots lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks class on the Learning Path.

      Curved path Flashcard for Babies

      One long curved path sweeping across the card. Following a single line from one end to the other is real eye work — and the start of how reading will one day feel.

      Why black and white works

      Sends the gaze on one long journey across the page and safely back again.

      Show it slowly

      Run a finger along the curve from end to end while your baby follows.

      What it builds

      Tracking one continuous line builds the sustained gaze that stories will ask for.

      Print it like this

      Sturdy cardstock works best, since this one lives on the floor.

      Baby tip

      Start at the same end each time — predictability helps young eyes.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Curved path lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks class on the Learning Path.

      Red circle Flashcard for Babies

      The first colour card of the set: one big red circle. Red is the colour young babies notice first, which makes this the gentlest possible bridge from black and white into colour.

      Why black and white works

      Introduces colour gently, since red is the first shade young eyes truly notice.

      Show it slowly

      Hold it close after a feed and simply say red, then wait quietly.

      What it builds

      A single bold shade wakes colour cells that monochrome pages left resting.

      Print it like this

      White cardstock keeps the red reading as one single shape.

      Baby tip

      One colour word per card is enough at this stage.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Red circle lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks class on the Learning Path.

      Red and black Flashcard for Babies

      A card that pairs strong red with bold black, joining the two worlds your baby now sees. The familiar contrast is still there — with one big new colour folded in.

      Why black and white works

      Bridges the black-and-white world and the brand-new colour world on one page.

      Show it slowly

      Touch the red part, then a black part, giving each its own slow word.

      What it builds

      Swinging attention between two colours builds flexibility and early comparing.

      Print it like this

      Standard photo size on cardstock slips neatly into most card holders.

      Baby tip

      Name red first; it is the newer, more exciting discovery.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Red and black lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks class on the Learning Path.

      Red face detail Flashcard for Babies

      A face with a bold red detail, bringing the set full circle: faces, patterns and colour in one last card. A friendly finish for the Newborn 2 stage.

      Why black and white works

      Closes the set by folding colour into a face, your baby's favourite picture of all.

      Show it slowly

      Show it at cot side before a nap, letting the day's last look be easy.

      What it builds

      Finding one red detail inside a bigger picture builds early visual search.

      Print it like this

      Print alongside the earlier faces so your baby can revisit old friends.

      Baby tip

      Finish the set softly; a quiet ending keeps looking a lovely habit.

      Teach it, step by step

      Want the full walkthrough? Open the Red face detail lesson on the Learning Path.

      From the Faces & Visual Tracking for Babies 6–12 Weeks class on the Learning Path.
